figures.caption: Figure 1: The geometry of a single-neuron dose. Because the write direction v̂ is orthogonal to the residual rL, the dose tv builds a right triangle whose hypotenuse is the perturbed residual r(t) = rL + tv (Equation 1). Increasing the dose rotates r(t) from rL toward v̂. The control coordinate cos θv (Equation 2) is the cosine of the angle θv between r(t) and v̂, and the coupling g = t/B (Equation 3) is the tangent of the rotation angle φ away from rL. The dose t = B is the 45◦ point where the write matches the residual.

Table 1: Notation. The control window is one inequality on one coordinate: coherent control exists when the behavior trigger lies below the collapse ceiling, cos θtrigv (τ) < cos θcollv . Geometry sets cos θv; the budget and collapse coefficient set its scale; the trigger is behavior-set.

Figure 2: The control window on a benign, judge-free behavior. An operator neuron (Llama L19/F13312) is dosed on symbolic arithmetic a + b= and scored by exact match: addition (gray) holds below the trigger, the neuron switches addition to multiplication (+→×, green) sharply from cos θv ≈ 0.3, and the output begins to collapse at the largest doses shown (cos θv ≈ 0.75), approaching the ceiling near 0.84 (red). The exact oracle needs no coherence gate, isolating the window from the measurement corrections that safety behaviors require (Section 3.4).
Table 2: The measurement contract: the five conventions under which a control window is measured. Artifact analysis and judge details are in Appendix E.

Figure 3: Collapse is universal in the rescaled coupling. (a) Coherence, the distinct-bigram ratio, against the coupling g = t/B for the held-out neurons across six architectures; the collapse transition is scattered, near g ≈ 1.5 for the Qwen and Llama families and ≈ 0.3 for Gemma. (b) Rescaling the coupling by each model’s single constant m∗ collapses every curve onto one cliff at x = 1 (shaded band). The dashed line is the 0.30 coherence floor.

Table 3: Collapse coefficient m∗ = t∗/B on held-out neurons, by architecture, with the median participation ratio (PR) of the residual. Across eight architectures m∗ tracks PR (Spearman 0.67): the seven distributed-residual models occupy a robust band, and Gemma’s near-rank-one residual makes it five times more fragile. Mistral and Phi are held-out families; Phi shows that a concentrated residual (PR 5.4) is still robust, so the fragility is the near-rank-one limit, not low PR in general.

Figure 4: The collapse coefficient tracks residual concentration across eight architectures (Spearman 0.67). The seven distributed-residual models occupy a robust band (m∗ ≈ 1.4 to 1.8); only Gemma’s near-rank-one residual makes it fragile. Phi (held out, diamond) has a concentrated, massive-activation residual (PR 5.4) yet is robust, so the fragility is the near-rank-one limit, not low PR in general. Stars in Table 3 mark the held-out families.

Table 4: Prospective control-window test, summary (per-neuron predictions and dosed outcomes for all fifteen are in Table 10). Every prediction was committed from weights and behavior class before dosing, then scored blind. The continuous ceiling error, not the verdict count, is the prospective result.

Figure 5: Recall is cheap; precision is the law. (a) The contrastive screen ranks all 301,056 band neurons by |∆a|; the six genuine refusal pivots (stars; green actionable, olive coherent-bypass-only) all fall in the top fifty, the top 0.017%. Salience is not control: the single highest-|∆a| neuron (red, L26/F7711) is window-closed. (b) On the eighteen further high-|∆a| candidates beyond those six validated pivots, the window law rejects thirteen and the strict actionable judge rejects the remaining five, so no additional |∆a| false positive survives both filters.

Figure 7: Coherent bypass is not actionable reach. Each point is one audited refusal pivot, both axes scored on the same n = 24 requests (bars: Wilson 95%): the horizontal axis is coherent bypass (full-reply coherence-gated non-refusal, Claude-Haiku), the vertical axis is strict-actionable content (register-aware four-way judge, peak over rollout depth). The dotted diagonal is the hypothesis that bypass equals reach; points fall well below it. L16/F6950 reaches coherent bypass 0.62 yet 0.00 actionable (non-overlapping intervals), and bypass does not order reach: L15/F9635 matches its 0.62 bypass at 0.17 actionable, while L10/F1084 bypasses at 0.96 for 0.75. The three genuine-actionable Llama pivots (green) lie near the top, the coherent-bypass-only pivots (blue) on the floor, and the Qwen proxies (orange) near the origin. The decoupling is the safety-level instance of “leverage is not reach.”

Figure 8: Behavior-specific rollout horizon. Onset time τ∗(cos θv) for the operator neuron (L19/F13312, blue) and the language-routing neuron (L25/F347, orange), log scale. The operator floors at τ∗ = 8 and cannot be made earlier by dose; language is token-local (τ∗ = 1) inside the window and its onset diverges only as the dose approaches the trigger boundary near cos θv ≈ 0.18. Per-behavior surfaces and bootstrap intervals are in Appendix C.1.

Figure 9: Harm commits late, then plateaus. Strict-actionable rate as a function of rollout depth τ (a cumulative prefix-audit; the τ=256 generation is a verified prefix-superset of τ=128) for the genuine Llama refusal pivots of Section 6. The rate rises, plateaus by τ ≈ 96 to 128 (the harm horizon), and holds flat to τ=256 with no late collapse; the plateau height is the pivot’s semantic potency. Coherent-bypass-only pivots stay at zero on this axis at every depth.

Table 6: The law explains and extends prior single-neuron findings. Each prior result is one point on the control window; the law adds a controller or a correction, named by the specific neuron and model (identified in this work unless cited otherwise).

Figure 10: Control windows, one representative controller per behavior class. Each panel plots the behavior metric (red) and coherence, the distinct-bigram ratio (blue), against the control coordinate cos θv; the dotted line is the 0.30 coherence floor and the dashed lines the ±0.83 collapse guides. A language router (L25/F347) and an operator gate (L19/F13312) trigger sharply near cos θv ≈ 0.3 with wide coherent windows; a coarse safety decision (L27/F13025) triggers softly with a narrower window; the Gemma safety neuron (L25/F1790) collapses before any trigger, the closed-window case. Behavior must be read with coherence: at the window edges the behavior detector alone overcounts. The full eleven-controller set is Figure 14 in the appendix.

Table 7: Measured control windows. Mode switches open wide windows with sharp triggers near 0.3; coarse decisions open narrow windows with soft triggers near 0.45; Gemma’s safety neuron is window-closed (ceiling below any trigger). L11/F4258 is open once dosed in budget units (Section 9).
Table 8: Collapse coefficient m∗ = t∗/B on 24 held-out neurons per model: mean, coefficient of variation, within-model R2 of collapse dose against B, and median residual participation ratio.

Figure 11: The universal drive, measured versus predicted. Points are the measured control coordinate (midpoint of the six-model range, error bars the range) at each coupling g; the line is the geometric prediction cos θv = g/ √ 1 + g2. The range is at most 0.02 at every dose, so the drive is architecture-independent.
Table 9: Cross-architecture single-neuron control. “safety” = coherent refusal bypass; “modeswitch” = routing or operator flip; window status is the dominant verdict for that model.

Figure 12: A single neuron’s reach under pinning versus residual injection, as the control coordinate cos θv actually reached (mean over generic prompts). Left, pinning the neuron’s own activation: on the pre-norm Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen3.5-2B the neuron drives cos θv across the full range to ±0.99, past the refusal trigger (dashed, cos θv=0.45); on Gemma-3-4B all four refusal neurons saturate at cos θv ≤ 0.19 and never approach the trigger, because Gemma’s post-FFN RMSNorm renormalizes the FFN output and caps the whole block’s contribution to a small fraction of the residual norm. Right, injecting the write directly into the residual: the coordinate follows the universal drive on every architecture, reaching cos θv ≈ 0.9, so the cap is specific to what a neuron can do, not to the coordinate. Pinning and injection therefore coincide for pre-norm models but diverge on Gemma. The vertical axis is the coordinate reached, not coherence: injection drives Gemma’s cos θv high but the output collapses by cos θv ≈ 0.3 (the m∗=0.31 ceiling), so neither pinning (which cannot reach the trigger) nor injection (which collapses before it) coherently steers a Gemma refusal neuron.

Table 10: Full prospective sweep, fifteen held-out safety neurons over five architectures, all predictions committed before dosing. “P”/“O” are predicted/observed. A dash in cos θtrigv marks a closed or artifact outcome with no coherent trigger. Bold marks the law’s informative edges: the two closed mechanisms (geometric on Gemma, decoupled at extreme depth) and the recovered dosing artifact. Ceiling MAE = 0.14 (bootstrap 95% CI 0.09–0.23); bulk (depth ≤ 0.8) MAE ≈ 0.07.

Figure 13: Control surfaces. Top: operator (L19/F13312) heatmap C(cos θv, τ) with a hard onset floor at τ = 8 and total collapse at cos θv = 0.90. Bottom: language (L25/F347) boundary zoom, token-local in the window with a diverging onset at the trigger edge. Each row pairs the heatmap (left) with the onset curve τ∗(cos θv) (right).

Table 12: A working taxonomy of the observed single-neuron control and failure modes, one row per behavior we probed. It is an empirical map of the cases we measured, not a claim that these are the only modes.

Figure 14: Control windows for eleven controllers across three behavior classes (full set; the representative subset is Figure 10). Each panel plots the behavior metric (red) and coherence, the distinct-bigram ratio (blue), against the control coordinate cos θv; the dotted line is the 0.30 coherence floor and the dashed lines the ±0.83 collapse guides.

Figure 15: Framing controllers obey the control window. Response uniformity (template lock-in on benign arithmetic prompts, a judge-free oracle) against the control coordinate | cos θv| on each neuron’s controlling sign, for the three confirmed Qwen3.5-2B framing controllers. The template locks in, crossing the 0.8 controller bar, across a trigger band near | cos θv| ≈ 0.6 (shaded), higher than the mode-switch trigger (≈ 0.3) and refusal (≈ 0.45); coherence does not collapse in range, so the window is open. L8/F3742 is the math-refusal controller (“mathematically impossible” on a simple sum).

Figure 16: Inside the window the dose preserves task-local capability. For the benign mode-switch neurons (operator +→×, L19/F13312; language EN→ZH, L25/F347), the behavior rate (leverage), the capability rate (reach: on-target and non-degenerate), and character diversity vs the control coordinate cos θv . Capability is high and flat from the trigger across the controlling (−v) window and is zero on the non-controlling branch. For the language router the curves separate at the ceiling (the dose still routes the language while the text collapses), making “leverage is not reach” quantitative; for the operator, whose detector requires a coherent correct product, behavior and capability coincide and fall together at the ceiling.

Figure 17: Negative result. Foot versus knee, branch-resolved, at τ=1: branch resolution removes the apparent universal over-prediction but does not yield a trigger law. On the controlling branch the tanh/knee fit (solid) crosses M=0 near the measured trigger for the language router and the refusalbypass pivots; the origin quadratic (dashed) reads the flat foot and overshoots. The off-axis operator (L19/F13312) never crosses (its margin stays below zero across the dose range). The dramatic “always over-predicts” of a sign-averaged silent fit is thus largely a branch-resolution artifact.

Figure 18: Negative result. Rollout-indexed trigger: rollout feedback helps token-local cases but does not give a universal trigger predictor. The first-token estimate cpred(τ=1) over-shoots; fitting the same margin along the free rollout converges toward the measured trigger, while a teacher-forced undosed prefix stays at the foot—so where a rollout effect exists it is autoregressive prefix feedback. Clean for the language router; the refusal-bypass safety read is reliable only at short horizons (the trigger collapses at τ≥32 from a non-refusal detector over-count on long generations).

Figure 19: Negative result. Amplification is behavior-specific, so no single kernel predicts the trigger. The effective-curvature kernel G(τ) = βeff(τ)/βeff(1) rises for the language router (A > 0) but attenuates for the refusal-bypass pivots (A < 0), so a single amplification kernel is not universal. Exploratory; motivates the two-regime conclusion.

Table 15: Census of featured single-neuron cases, grouped by gate type, with model and one example each. Safety examples are content-free; the row-level content audit is Appendix D.1 and the fifteen held-out validation neurons are Table 10. All neurons were identified in this work except the published refusal neuron L11/F4258 [Kazemi et al., 2026] and the super weight [Yu et al., 2025].
